claim: GABAA receptor (GABAAR) pentamers are assembled from a pool of 19 subunits.
source: GABAA receptor (GABAAR) pentamers are assembled from a pool of 19 subunits, and variety in subunit combinations diversifies GABAAR functions to tune brain activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background information.

claim: Variety in subunit combinations diversifies GABAAR functions to tune brain activity.
source: GABAA receptor (GABAAR) pentamers are assembled from a pool of 19 subunits, and variety in subunit combinations diversifies GABAAR functions to tune brain activity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Pentamers with distinct subunit compositions localize differentially at synaptic and non-synaptic sites to mediate phasic and tonic inhibition, respectively.
source: Pentamers with distinct subunit compositions localize differentially at synaptic and non-synaptic sites to mediate phasic and tonic inhibition, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Despite multitudes of theoretical permutations, limited subunit combinations have been identified in the brain.
source: Despite multitudes of theoretical permutations, limited subunit combinations have been identified in the brain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: α subunits possess intrinsic signals to segregate into distinct pentamers.
source: First, α subunits possess intrinsic signals to segregate into distinct pentamers.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figures 2C, 2D, and 6F.

claim: γ2 is essential for GABAAR assembly with Neuroligin-2 (NL2) and GARLHs.
source: Second, γ2 is essential for GABAAR assembly with Neuroligin-2 (NL2) and GARLHs, which localize GABAARs at synapses.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: GARLHs and NL2 localize GABAARs at synapses.
source: Second, γ2 is essential for GABAAR assembly with Neuroligin-2 (NL2) and GARLHs, which localize GABAARs at synapses.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: δ suppresses α6 synaptic localization by preventing assembly with GARLHs/NL2.
source: Third, δ suppresses α6 synaptic localization by preventing assembly with GARLHs/NL2.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Fast inhibition of synaptic membrane depolarization is mediated principally by the binding of GABA to ionotropic GABA receptors (GABAARs).
source: In the brain, fast inhibition of synaptic membrane depolarization is mediated principally by the binding of GABA to ionotropic GABA receptors (GABAARs), hetero- or homo-pentamers consisting of combinations of six α, three β and ten non-α/β subunits (Barnard et al., 1998; Olsen and Sieghart, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: GABAARs are hetero- or homo-pentamers consisting of combinations of six α, three β and ten non-α/β subunits.
source: In the brain, fast inhibition of synaptic membrane depolarization is mediated principally by the binding of GABA to ionotropic GABA receptors (GABAARs), hetero- or homo-pentamers consisting of combinations of six α, three β and ten non-α/β subunits (Barnard et al., 1998; Olsen and Sieghart, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: Only a fraction of theoretically possible GABAAR permutations are observed in neural tissues.
source: While a huge number of permutations are theoretically possible, only a fraction are observed in neural tissues, with just a handful of major GABAAR subtypes dominating (Barnard et al., 1998; McKernan and Whiting, 1996; Olsen and Sieghart, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: In cerebellar granule cells, α1/β/γ2-containing GABAARs localize at synapses and mediate phasic inhibition.
source: For example, in cerebellar granule cells, α1/β/γ2-containing GABAARs localize at synapses and mediate phasic inhibition, whereas α6/β/δ-containing GABAARs localize at extrasynaptic sites and mediate tonic inhibition (Günther et al., 1995; Jones et al., 1997; Mihalek et al., 1999; Nusser et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: In cerebellar granule cells, α6/β/δ-containing GABAARs localize at extrasynaptic sites and mediate tonic inhibition.
source: For example, in cerebellar granule cells, α1/β/γ2-containing GABAARs localize at synapses and mediate phasic inhibition, whereas α6/β/δ-containing GABAARs localize at extrasynaptic sites and mediate tonic inhibition (Günther et al., 1995; Jones et al., 1997; Mihalek et al., 1999; Nusser et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: The major GABAAR subtypes contain at most one non-α/β subunit, making non-α/β subunits mutually exclusive within a pentamer.
source: For example, the major GABAAR subtypes contain at most one non-α/β subunit, making non-α/β subunits mutually exclusive within a pentamer (Araujo et al., 1998; Jechlinger et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: The majority of GABAAR pentamers incorporate two α subunits of a single isoform.
source: By contrast, it remains unclear how the majority of GABAAR pentamers incorporate two α subunits of a single isoform (Barnard et al., 1998), or which non-α/β subunit dictates pentamer assembly of each α and β isoform in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to prior work.

claim: AMPA receptors form a complex with TARP auxiliary subunits, which are required for AMPA receptor synaptic localization.
source: AMPA receptors form a complex with TARP auxiliary subunits, which are required for AMPA receptor synaptic localization.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: GARLH putative auxiliary subunits of GABAARs were recently identified in the brain.
source: Similarly, GARLH putative auxiliary subunits of GABAARs were recently identified in the brain (Yamasaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work by the same authors.

claim: GARLHs form complexes with GABAARs and the inhibitory synaptic cell adhesion molecule Neuroligin-2 (NL2).
source: GARLHs form complexes with GABAARs and the inhibitory synaptic cell adhesion molecule Neuroligin-2 (NL2), and are essential for synaptic localization and inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs), but not GABAAR activity at the cell surface in primary hippocampal neurons and the hippocampus.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work by the same authors.

claim: GARLHs are essential for synaptic localization and inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs), but not GABAAR activity at the cell surface in primary hippocampal neurons and the hippocampus.
source: GARLHs form complexes with GABAARs and the inhibitory synaptic cell adhesion molecule Neuroligin-2 (NL2), and are essential for synaptic localization and inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs), but not GABAAR activity at the cell surface in primary hippocampal neurons and the hippocampus.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work by the same authors.

claim: Synaptic localization of the inhibitory scaffolding molecule gephyrin requires GARLH expression in hippocampus.
source: Furthermore, synaptic localization of the inhibitory scaffolding molecule gephyrin requires GARLH expression in hippocampus (Yamasaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work by the same authors.

claim: All δ and most α6 migrated at 480 kDa on BN-PAGE in mouse cerebellar membranes.
source: We found that all δ and most α6 migrated at 480 kDa, whereas nearly all γ2 and most α1 migrated at 720 kDa (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the BN-PAGE experiment shown in Figure 1.

claim: Nearly all γ2 and most α1 migrated at 720 kDa on BN-PAGE in mouse cerebellar membranes.
source: We found that all δ and most α6 migrated at 480 kDa, whereas nearly all γ2 and most α1 migrated at 720 kDa (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the BN-PAGE experiment shown in Figure 1.

claim: β2/3 migrated equally at 480 and 720 kDa on BN-PAGE in mouse cerebellar membranes.
source: By contrast, β2/3 migrated equally at 480 and 720 kDa (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the BN-PAGE experiment shown in Figure 1.

claim: In the brain, GABAARs assemble with GARLHs and NL2 to form a tripartite complex that migrates at 720 kDa on BN-PAGE.
source: In the brain, GABAARs assemble with GARLHs and NL2 to form a tripartite complex that migrates at 720 kDa on BN-PAGE (Yamasaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work by the same authors.

claim: Both GARLH4 and NL2 co-migrated at 720 kDa on BN-PAGE in mouse cerebellar membranes.
source: Consistently, we found that both GARLH4 and NL2 also co-migrated at 720 kDa.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the BN-PAGE experiment shown in Figure 1.

claim: Endogenous GABAAR subunits segregate into two major complexes—a GARLH/NL2-associated (GARLHed) α1/β/γ2-containing complex migrating at 720 kDa, and a GARLHless α6/β/δ-containing GABAAR migrating at 480 kDa.
source: Thus, endogenous GABAAR subunits segregate into two major complexes—a GARLH/NL2-associated (GARLHed) α1/β/γ2-containing complex migrating at 720 kDa, and a GARLHless α6/β/δ-containing GABAAR migrating at 480 kDa (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 1.

claim: α1/β2 and α1/β2/HAγ2 hetero-oligomers migrate at 520 kDa on BN-PAGE in Xenopus laevis oocytes.
source: We observed α1/β2 and α1/β2/HAγ2 hetero-oligomers at 520 kDa, slightly higher than the 480 kDa complex in the brain (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the BN-PAGE experiment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The size difference between oocyte and brain GABAAR complexes on BN-PAGE may be caused by differences in species, alternative splicing or post-translational modification.
source: This size difference corresponds with differences in the molecular weights of the GABAAR subunits expressed in oocytes and in the brain on SDS-PAGE and may be caused by differences in species, alternative splicing or post-translational modification (Yamasaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed size difference.

claim: α1/β2- and α1/β2/γ2-mediated GABA-evoked currents were observed in Xenopus laevis oocytes.
source: Corresponding to the 520 kDa complexes, we observed α1/β2- and α1/β2/γ2-mediated GABA-evoked currents (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Weakly expressed β2/HAγ2 hetero-oligomers were detected at 600 kDa on BN-PAGE in Xenopus laevis oocytes.
source: In addition, we detected weakly expressed β2/HAγ2 hetero-oligomers at 600 kDa (Figure 2A) and tiny β2/γ2-mediated GABA-evoked currents (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), whereas neither α1, β2 nor HAγ2 homomers were detected (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the BN-PAGE experiment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Neither α1, β2 nor HAγ2 homomers were detected in Xenopus laevis oocytes.
source: In addition, we detected weakly expressed β2/HAγ2 hetero-oligomers at 600 kDa (Figure 2A) and tiny β2/γ2-mediated GABA-evoked currents (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), whereas neither α1, β2 nor HAγ2 homomers were detected (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: An α1/HAβ2/γ2 GABAAR oligomer and a concatenated pentamer, HAβ2-α1-HAβ2-α1-γ2 (HA2Pent), migrated at 520 kDa on BN-PAGE.
source: On BN-PAGE, HA2Pent migrated at 520 kDa, similar to α1/HAβ2/γ2 GABAARs, although the signal was weak, likely due to a difference in pentamer expression levels and HA epitope accessibility (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the BN-PAGE experiment shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The 520 kDa complex in cRNA-injected oocytes consists of a GABAAR pentamer.
source: Thus, we concluded that the 520 kDa complex in cRNA-injected oocytes consists of a GABAAR pentamer.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of oligomers and concatenated pentamers shown in Figure 2B.

claim: α1 and α6 preferentially incorporate into GARLHed and GARLHless GABAAR complexes, respectively, and thus are largely segregated in vivo.
source: Consistent with this, we found that α1 and α6 preferentially incorporate into GARLHed and GARLHless GABAAR complexes, respectively, and thus are largely segregated in vivo (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 1.

claim: α1 and HAα6 segregate independent of non-α/β subunits when co-expressed with β2 in Xenopus laevis oocytes.
source: The results indicate that α1 and HAα6 segregate independent of non-α/β subunits when co-expressed with β2, and thus their segregation is encoded by the α subunits themselves.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the antibody shift assay shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The segregation of α1 and α6 is encoded by the α subunits themselves.
source: The results indicate that α1 and HAα6 segregate independent of non-α/β subunits when co-expressed with β2, and thus their segregation is encoded by the α subunits themselves.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the antibody shift assay shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In vivo, the segregation of α1 and α6 into distinct GABAAR complexes is independent of γ2 and δ.
source: Thus, in vivo, the segregation of α1 and α6 into distinct GABAAR complexes is independent of γ2 and δ.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the antibody shift assay in γ2/δ GC-DKO cerebella shown in Figure 2D.

claim: All α1 and β2 assemble with γ2 in the oocyte system when γ2 is coexpressed.
source: By contrast, when γ2 was coexpressed with α1 and β2, the three subunits formed a 520 kDa GABAAR that was completely supershifted by the anti-γ2 antibody (Figure 3A), indicating that all α1 and β2 assemble with γ2 in our oocyte system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the antibody shift assay shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Most of the GARLHed complexes in the cerebellum contain γ2.
source: These results suggest that most of the GARLHed complexes and GARLHless GABAARs in the cerebellum contain γ2 and δ,respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the antibody shift assay shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Most of the GARLHless GABAARs in the cerebellum contain δ.
source: These results suggest that most of the GARLHed complexes and GARLHless GABAARs in the cerebellum contain γ2 and δ,respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the antibody shift assay shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In Gabrg2fl/fl cultures expressing CreERT, both γ2 expression and GARLHed complexes were eliminated.
source: On the other hand, in Gabrg2fl/fl cultures expressing CreERT, both γ2 expression and GARLHed complexes were eliminated (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the BN-PAGE experiment shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The association of native GABAARs with GARLHs requires γ2.
source: Combining our new finding that γ2 is required in vivo for assembling the native GABAAR complex (Figure 3C) with the finding from Yamasaki et al. (2017) that γ2 is required for reconstituting the native GABAAR complex in a heterologous system, we conclude that the association of native GABAARs with GARLHs requires γ2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 3C combined with prior work.

claim: γ2 is required for GABAAR synaptic localization in cultured cortical neurons.
source: γ2 is required for GABAAR synaptic localization in cultured cortical neurons (Essrich et al., 1998) and neonatal dorsal root ganglion neurons (Günther et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: γ2 is required for GABAAR synaptic localization in neonatal dorsal root ganglion neurons.
source: γ2 is required for GABAAR synaptic localization in cultured cortical neurons (Essrich et al., 1998) and neonatal dorsal root ganglion neurons (Günther et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: In γ2 GC-KO mice, the protein levels of GARLH4 and NL2 are reduced in total cerebellar lysate.
source: We previously showed that in γ2 GC-KO mice, the protein levels of GARLH4 and NL2 are reduced in total cerebellar lysate, while the protein levels of GARLH4, NL2 and α1 are reduced in the glomerular postsynapse-enriched fraction (Yamasaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work by the same authors.

claim: In γ2 GC-KO mice, the protein levels of GARLH4, NL2 and α1 are reduced in the glomerular postsynapse-enriched fraction.
source: We previously showed that in γ2 GC-KO mice, the protein levels of GARLH4 and NL2 are reduced in total cerebellar lysate, while the protein levels of GARLH4, NL2 and α1 are reduced in the glomerular postsynapse-enriched fraction (Yamasaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work by the same authors.

claim: Loss of γ2 expression was observed specifically in the granular layer in γ2 GC-KO mice.
source: We confirmed loss of γ2 expression specifically in the granular layer of adult γ2 GC-KO mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Overall intensity of α1 and β2 signal was not noticeably altered in γ2 GC-KO mice.
source: By contrast, overall intensity of α1 and β2 signal was not noticeably altered (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In γ2 GC-KO mice, the fraction of α1 colocalized with VGAT was substantially reduced.
source: By contrast, in the γ2 GC-KO mice, the fraction of α1 colocalized with VGAT was substantially reduced, while the fraction of GluN1 colocalized with α1 was substantially increased (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: In γ2 GC-KO mice, the fraction of GluN1 colocalized with α1 was substantially increased.
source: By contrast, in the γ2 GC-KO mice, the fraction of α1 colocalized with VGAT was substantially reduced, while the fraction of GluN1 colocalized with α1 was substantially increased (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: GABAAR-mediated sIPSCs were almost completely eliminated in γ2 GC-KO mice.
source: GABAAR-mediated sIPSCs were almost completely eliminated in γ2 GC-KO mice (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: The rare residual sIPSCs in γ2 GC-KO mice displayed decreased amplitude.
source: The rare residual sIPSCs in γ2 GC-KO mice displayed decreased amplitude (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The vast majority of GABAAR-mediated synaptic events require γ2.
source: The results indicate that the vast majority of GABAAR-mediated synaptic events require γ2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: In the γ2 GC-KO, the fraction of gephyrin co-localized with VGAT was substantially reduced.
source: By contrast, in the γ2 GC-KO mice, the fraction of gephyrin co-localized with VGAT was substantially reduced and the fraction of GluN1 signal co-localized with gephyrin was substantially reduced. (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: In the γ2 GC-KO, the fraction of GluN1 signal co-localized with gephyrin was substantially reduced.
source: By contrast, in the γ2 GC-KO mice, the fraction of gephyrin co-localized with VGAT was substantially reduced and the fraction of GluN1 signal co-localized with gephyrin was substantially reduced. (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: γ2 directs the synaptic localization of gephyrin in the adult brain.
source: Thus, γ2 directs the synaptic localization of gephyrin in the adult brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: In δ KO cerebellar granule cells, an increase in the frequency and furosemide sensitivity of GABAAR-mediated miniature IPSCs (mIPSCs) was reported.
source: Interestingly, in δ KO cerebellar granule cells, an increase in the frequency and furosemide sensitivity of GABAAR-mediated miniature IPSCs (mIPSCs) was reported (Accardi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Weaker α6 signal was observed in three δ GC-KO cerebella consistently by immunohistochemistry.
source: On the other hand, we observed weaker α6 signal in three δ GC-KO cerebella consistently by immunohistochemistry (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5A.

claim: An absence of α6 signal was observed in conventional α6 KO cerebellum.
source: To confirm the specificity of the α6 signal, we obtained conventional α6 KO cerebellum (Aller et al., 2003), in which we observed an absence of α6 signal (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In δ GC-KO mice, α6 formed clusters at the glomerular periphery that substantially overlapped with VGAT.
source: High-magnification images revealed that, in δ GC-KO mice, α6 formed clusters at the glomerular periphery that substantially overlapped with VGAT (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In control littermates, α6 signal was diffuse and overlapped with GluN1 signal.
source: By contrast, in control littermates, α6 signal was diffuse and overlapped with GluN1 signal (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The fraction of α6 co-localized with VGAT was substantially increased in the granular layer of δ GC-KO mice.
source: The fraction of α6 co-localized with VGAT was substantially increased in the granular layer of δ GC-KO mice, whereas the fraction of the entire glomerular marker GluN1 colocalized with α6 was reduced (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The fraction of the entire glomerular marker GluN1 colocalized with α6 was reduced in δ GC-KO mice.
source: The fraction of α6 co-localized with VGAT was substantially increased in the granular layer of δ GC-KO mice, whereas the fraction of the entire glomerular marker GluN1 colocalized with α6 was reduced (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 5C.

claim: δ suppresses synaptic localization of α6 in the brain.
source: These results indicate that δ suppresses synaptic localization of α6 in the brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: α6 incorporates into GARLHed complexes in cerebella from δ GC-KO mice.
source: Most strikingly, α6 incorporated into GARLHed complexes in cerebella from δ GC-KO mice, whereas α6 incorporated into GARLHless GABAARs in cerebella from control, γ2 GC-KO and γ2/δ GC-DKO mice, on BN-PAGE (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the BN-PAGE experiment shown in Figure 6A.

claim: α6 incorporated into GARLHless GABAARs in cerebella from control, γ2 GC-KO and γ2/δ GC-DKO mice.
source: Most strikingly, α6 incorporated into GARLHed complexes in cerebella from δ GC-KO mice, whereas α6 incorporated into GARLHless GABAARs in cerebella from control, γ2 GC-KO and γ2/δ GC-DKO mice, on BN-PAGE (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the BN-PAGE experiment shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The α6-containing GARLHed complex in δ GC-KO cerebella was eliminated in γ2/δ GC-DKO cerebella.
source: The α6-containing GARLHed complex in δ GC-KO cerebella was eliminated in γ2/δ GC-DKO cerebella, supporting the earlier finding that γ2 is required for formation of the GARLHed complex (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the BN-PAGE experiment shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In δ GC-KO cerebella, the amount of γ2 and NL2 in GARLHed complexes was increased relative to controls.
source: In δ GC-KO cerebella, the amount of γ2 and NL2 in GARLHed complexes was increased relative to controls (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the BN-PAGE experiment shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: In δ GC-KO cerebellum, all the essential components of GARLHed complexes—GARLH4, NL2 and γ2—were upregulated without concomitant upregulation of α1, while α6 was only slightly decreased.
source: Consistent with this, in δ GC-KO cerebellum, all the essential components of GARLHed complexes—GARLH4, NL2 and γ2—were upregulated without concomitant upregulation of α1, while α6 was only slightly decreased (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the western blot analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: An increase in α1 and γ2 in GARLHless GABAARs on BN-PAGE was observed in δ GC-KO cerebella.
source: We also observed an increase in α1 and γ2 in GARLHless GABAARs on BN-PAGE in δ GC-KO cerebella, implying that in δ GC-KO cerebella, GARLH4 and/or NL2 becomes limiting for the GARLHed complex (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the BN-PAGE experiment shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: In δ GC-KO cerebella, GARLH4 and/or NL2 becomes limiting for the GARLHed complex.
source: We also observed an increase in α1 and γ2 in GARLHless GABAARs on BN-PAGE in δ GC-KO cerebella, implying that in δ GC-KO cerebella, GARLH4 and/or NL2 becomes limiting for the GARLHed complex (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: δ inhibits the incorporation of α6 into γ2-containing GARLHed complexes in vivo.
source: Together, these results suggest that δ inhibits the incorporation of α6 into γ2-containing GARLHed complexes in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: δ is sufficient to inhibit α6 incorporation into γ2-containing GABAARs in heterologous cells.
source: We next confirmed that δ is sufficient to inhibit α6 incorporation into γ2-containing GABAARs in heterologous cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the antibody shift assay shown in Figure 6D.

claim: GABAARs associated with GARLH4/NL2, regardless of whether α1 or α6 was expressed, when coexpressed with γ2, but not δ in oocytes.
source: We found that GABAARs associated with GARLH4/NL2, regardless of whether α1 or α6 was expressed, when coexpressed with γ2, but not δ (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the BN-PAGE experiment shown in Figure 6E.

claim: α1 and α6 remain largely segregated into separate complexes, even when both assemble with GARLH/NL2.
source: This suggests that α1 and α6 remain largely segregated into separate complexes, even when both assemble with GARLH/NL2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the antibody shift assay shown in Figure 6F.

claim: There is an assembly pathway for α6-containing GARLHed complexes that is normally silenced by δ.
source: These rules reveal the presence of an assembly pathway for α6-containing GARLHed complexes that is normally silenced by δ (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective data presented in the study.

claim: In the absence of δ, the α6-containing GARLHed assembly pathway serves to increase inhibitory synaptic transmission.
source: In the absence of δ, this pathway serves to increase inhibitory synaptic transmission (Accardi et al., 2015) by allowing α6-containing pentamers to assemble with GARLH/NL2 and localize to synapses (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective data presented in the study combined with prior work.

claim: In the absence of δ, α6-containing pentamers assemble with GARLH/NL2 and localize to synapses.
source: In the absence of δ, this pathway serves to increase inhibitory synaptic transmission (Accardi et al., 2015) by allowing α6-containing pentamers to assemble with GARLH/NL2 and localize to synapses (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective data presented in the study.

claim: Upregulation of γ2 in conventional δ KO mice was previously reported.
source: Upregulation of γ2 in conventional δ KO mice was previously reported (Tretter et al., 2001), which we also observed in the δ GC-KO mice (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work and confirmed by data in Figure 6C.

claim: α1 and β3 were increased in conventional δ KO mice.
source: α1 and β3 were increased in conventional δ KO mice (Tretter et al., 2001) but were not changed in our cerebellar granule cell-specific δ KO mice (Figure 6C), perhaps because Cre expression under the Gabra6 promoter is delayed until around P7.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: α1 and β3 were not changed in cerebellar granule cell-specific δ KO mice.
source: α1 and β3 were increased in conventional δ KO mice (Tretter et al., 2001) but were not changed in our cerebellar granule cell-specific δ KO mice (Figure 6C), perhaps because Cre expression under the Gabra6 promoter is delayed until around P7.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the western blot analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Cre expression under the Gabra6 promoter is delayed until around P7.
source: α1 and β3 were increased in conventional δ KO mice (Tretter et al., 2001) but were not changed in our cerebellar granule cell-specific δ KO mice (Figure 6C), perhaps because Cre expression under the Gabra6 promoter is delayed until around P7.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for the observed difference.

claim: A marked increase in α6-containing GABAAR-mediated IPSCs in cerebellar granule cells was observed in δ KO mice.
source: Supporting this, a marked increase in α6-containing GABAAR-mediated IPSCs in cerebellar granule cells was observed in δ KO mice (Accardi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Changes in δ expression could control the ratio of GARLHed complexes and GARLHless pentamers in vivo, and thus alter inhibitory synaptic strength.
source: This suggests the intriguing hypothesis that changes in δ expression—for example, by ethanol or seizure activity (Cagetti et al., 2003; Liang et al., 2006; Marutha Ravindran et al., 2007; Peng et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2007)—could control the ratio of GARLHed complexes and GARLHless pentamers in vivo, and thus alter inhibitory synaptic strength.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the findings of the study.

claim: BN-PAGE preserves protein complexes but cannot accurately measure their molecular weights, because in contrast to SDS-PAGE, protein complex structure affects migration on BN-PAGE.
source: BN-PAGE preserves protein complexes but cannot accurately measure their molecular weights, because in contrast to SDS-PAGE, protein complex structure affects migration on BN-PAGE (Kim et al., 2010; Schägger et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: AMPA receptors lacking their N-terminal domains migrate at 55 kDa on SDS-PAGE, while a tetramer of these subunits migrates at 480 kDa on BN-PAGE, roughly twice the expected 220 kDa for a tetramer of 55 kDa subunits.
source: For example, AMPA receptors lacking their N-terminal domains migrate at 55 kDa on SDS-PAGE, while a tetramer of these subunits migrates at 480 kDa on BN-PAGE, roughly twice the expected 220 kDa for a tetramer of 55 kDa subunits (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as an example with a citation to prior work.

claim: Cerebellar granule cells predominantly express two distinct GABAAR subtypes: α1/β/γ2- and α6/β/δ-containing GABAARs.
source: As an in vivo model for GABAAR assembly, we focused on cerebellar granule cells, which predominantly express two distinct GABAAR subtypes: α1/β/γ2- and α6/β/δ-containing GABAARs (Jechlinger et al., 1998; Nusser et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: The subunit arrangement in the prototypical α1/β2/γ2 pentamer is thought to be β2-α1-β2-α1-γ2.
source: The subunit arrangement in the prototypical α1/β2/γ2 pentamer is thought to be β2-α1-β2-α1-γ2 (Baur et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to prior work.

claim: One model for the subunit order for the α6/β2/δ pentamer is β2-α6-δ-α6-β2, with δ situated between both α6 subunits.
source: For the α6/β2/δ pentamer, the situation is slightly different. One model for the subunit order for this pentamer is β2-α6-δ-α6-β2, with δ situated between both α6 subunits (Baur et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a model with a citation to prior work.

claim: A structural study of a β3 homopentamer lacking intracellular loops has provided critical information regarding the overall channel architecture, as well as atomic resolution descriptions of intersubunit β3-β3 contacts.
source: Thus far, a structural study of a β3 homopentamer lacking intracellular loops has provided critical information regarding the overall channel architecture, as well as atomic resolution descriptions of intersubunit β3-β3 contacts (Miller and Aricescu, 2014).

claim: Loss of gephyrin clustering was observed in γ2-null primary cortical neurons.
source: We also showed previously that GARLH is required for the synaptic clustering of the inhibitory scaffold gephyrin in the hippocampus (Yamasaki et al., 2017) and loss of gephyrin clustering was observed in γ2-null primary cortical neurons (Essrich et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: GARLH is required for the synaptic clustering of the inhibitory scaffold gephyrin in the hippocampus.
source: We also showed previously that GARLH is required for the synaptic clustering of the inhibitory scaffold gephyrin in the hippocampus (Yamasaki et al., 2017) and loss of gephyrin clustering was observed in γ2-null primary cortical neurons (Essrich et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work by the same authors.

claim: α4 is proposed to localize to extrasynaptic sites and also assembles with δ in hippocampus.
source: Similar to α6, α4 is proposed to localize to extrasynaptic sites and also assembles with δ in hippocampus (Jechlinger et al., 1998; Jones et al., 1997; Wongsamitkul et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: Accardi and colleagues reported an increase in mIPSC frequency, but not amplitude, in δ KO mice.

claim: Changes in δ expression occur by ethanol or seizure activity.
source: This suggests the intriguing hypothesis that changes in δ expression—for example, by ethanol or seizure activity (Cagetti et al., 2003; Liang et al., 2006; Marutha Ravindran et al., 2007; Peng et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2007)—could control the ratio of GARLHed complexes and GARLHless pentamers in vivo, and thus alter inhibitory synaptic strength.
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Conventional γ2 knockout (KO) mice show postnatal lethality.
source: Because conventional γ2 knockout (KO) mice show postnatal lethality (Günther et al., 1995), we crossed double conditional Gabrg2fl/fl/Gabrdfl/fl mice with transgenic mice expressing Cre recombinase under the Gabra6 promoter (Fünfschilling and Reichardt, 2002; Lee and Maguire, 2013; Schweizer et al., 2003) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) (see Materials and methods), resulting in viable γ2/δ granule cell (GC)-specific double knock out (DKO) mice that displayed no changes in body weight (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to prior work.

claim: γ2/δ granule cell (GC)-specific double knock out (DKO) mice are viable and display no changes in body weight.
source: Because conventional γ2 knockout (KO) mice show postnatal lethality (Günther et al., 1995), we crossed double conditional Gabrg2fl/fl/Gabrdfl/fl mice with transgenic mice expressing Cre recombinase under the Gabra6 promoter (Fünfschilling and Reichardt, 2002; Lee and Maguire, 2013; Schweizer et al., 2003) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) (see Materials and methods), resulting in viable γ2/δ granule cell (GC)-specific double knock out (DKO) mice that displayed no changes in body weight (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: γ2 GC-KO mice are viable with no change in body weight.
source: These mice are viable with no change in body weight (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In α6 KO mice, α6 was eliminated, δ was reduced 85% and β2/3 was reduced 60%, whereas α1, γ2 and the excitatory synapse marked PSD-95 were not significantly altered.
source: In α6 KO mice, α6 was eliminated, δ was reduced 85% and β2/3 was reduced 60%, whereas α1, γ2 and the excitatory synapse marked PSD-95 were not significantly altered.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the western blot analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A reduction in expression of δ and β2/3 in total cerebellar lysate from α6 KO mice was confirmed, as published previously.
source: In addition, a reduction in expression of δ and β2/3 in total cerebellar lysate (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and δ signal by immunohistochemistry (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) from α6 KO mice was confirmed, as published previously (Jones et al., 1997; Nusser et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and 1B, with citations to prior work.

claim: Both cerebella from γ2 GC-KO and γ2/δ GC-DKO mice showed only a partial reduction in γ2 protein and the GARLHed complex, because the γ2 subunit and GARLHed complexes are also expressed in non-granule cell cerebellar neurons, including Purkinje cells.
source: Both cerebella from γ2 GC-KO and γ2/δ GC-DKO mice showed only a partial reduction in γ2 protein and the GARLHed complex, because the γ2 subunit and GARLHed complexes are also expressed in non-granule cell cerebellar neurons, including Purkinje cells (Laurie et al., 1992) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed partial reduction, with a citation to prior work.
